overview:
Romania curls around the Carpathian Mountains in southeastern Europe, with the Danube River along its southern edge and the Black Sea to the east. It is the largest country in the region, about the size of Oregon, bordering Ukraine, Moldova, Bulgaria, Serbia, and Hungary.

About 19 million people live in Romania. Romanian is a Romance language descended from Latin, like French and Italian, which makes it unusual among Slavic and Hungarian-speaking neighbors. Bucharest, the capital, mixes grand nineteenth-century boulevards with vast concrete projects from the communist era, among them the Palace of the Parliament. Romania is a republic with an elected president and parliament, and it joined the European Union in 2007.

Transylvania, in the center, is a region of forested hills, fortified Saxon churches, and hilltop castles, one of which, Bran Castle, is linked in tourist legend to Dracula. Beyond the mountains lie wide farming plains where horse carts still share the roads with trucks.
landAndNature: The Carpathians sweep through Romania in a great arc, carpeted in beech and spruce and rising above 2,500 meters in the Făgăraș range. These forests hold the largest brown bear population in Europe outside Russia, thousands of animals, along with wolves, lynx, and wild boar, and shepherds still walk flocks up to summer pastures. Outside the mountains the land opens into the plains of Wallachia and Moldavia, thick with wheat and sunflowers. In the east the Danube finishes a journey of about 2,850 kilometers in a huge delta of reeds and shifting channels, where pelicans, egrets, and roughly 300 bird species nest and sturgeon still swim upstream. Mud volcanoes bubble in the hills near Buzău.
peopleAndCulture: Romanians share the country with Hungarian, Roma, and German-speaking communities, and many villages keep their own costumes and dances, some circling hand in hand, others in fast lines with stamping feet. Most people belong to the Romanian Orthodox Church. Food is filling: sarmale, cabbage rolls stuffed with pork and rice, mămăligă, a cornmeal porridge much like polenta, and sour soups called ciorbă. The painted monasteries of Bucovina are covered on the outside with bright biblical scenes from the 1500s. Romania gave the world the sculptor Constantin Brâncuși, the composer George Enescu, and the gymnast Nadia Comăneci, and soccer and handball fill its stadiums.
history: The Dacians lived here until Rome conquered them in 106 AD, and Roman settlers left behind the country's language and its name. Waves of migrating peoples followed, and the medieval principalities of Wallachia, Moldavia, and Transylvania took shape. Vlad the Impaler, a fifteenth-century Wallachian prince, later lent his family name, Dracula, to a British novel. Ottoman, Habsburg, and Russian power all pressed on these lands. Wallachia and Moldavia united in 1859, independence was recognized in 1878, and Transylvania joined in 1918. After World War II Romania became a communist state; Nicolae Ceaușescu ruled from 1965 with harsh controls and huge demolition projects until a revolution in December 1989 removed him. Democratic elections have been held since.
funFacts: The Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest is the heaviest building in the world, with more than a thousand rooms.
Nadia Comăneci scored the first perfect ten in Olympic gymnastics in 1976; the scoreboard could only display 1.00.
The Danube Delta grows a little larger every year as the river drops its silt into the Black Sea.
An old salt mine at Turda has been turned into an underground park with a Ferris wheel and rowing boats on a lake.
Timișoara was the first European city to light its streets with electric lamps, in 1884.
